passages.text: Hinge-Region O-Glycosylation of Human Immunoglobulin G3 (IgG3)*

Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is one of the most abundant proteins present in human serum and a fundamental component of the immune system. <sentence_start/>IgG3 represents ∼8% of the total amount of IgG in human serum and stands out from the other IgG subclasses because of its elongated hinge region and enhanced effector functions. <sentence_start/>This study reports partial O-glycosylation of the IgG3 hinge region, observed with nanoLC-ESI-IT-MS(/MS) analysis after proteolytic digestion. <sentence_start/>The repeat regions within the IgG3 hinge were found to be in part O-glycosylated at the threonine in the triple repeat motif. <sentence_start/>Non-, mono- and disialylated core 1-type O-glycans were detected in various IgG3 samples, both poly- and monoclonal. <sentence_start/>NanoLC-ESI-IT-MS/MS with electron transfer dissociation fragmentation and CE-MS/MS with CID fragmentation were used to determine the site of IgG3 O-glycosylation. <sentence_start/>The O-glycosylation site was further confirmed by the recombinant production of mutant IgG3 in which potential O-glycosylation sites had been knocked out.

For IgG3 samples from six donors we found similar O-glycan structures and site occupancies, whereas for the same samples the conserved N-glycosylation of the Fc CH2 domain showed considerable interindividual variation. <sentence_start/>The occupancy of each of the three O-glycosylation sites was found to be ∼10% in six serum-derived IgG3 samples and ∼13% in two monoclonal IgG3 allotypes.

Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is one of the most abundant proteins present in human serum and represents approximately three-quarters of the total serum immunoglobulin content (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" pmcid="PMC1579064" pmid="4182354" count="1">1</citation>). <sentence_start/>As the main mediator of humoral immunity and an important link between the adaptive and innate immune system, IgG is a fundamental component of the immune system. <sentence_start/>IgG consists of two heavy and light chains, linked by disulfide bonds. <sentence_start/>The protein can be subdivided into the antigen-binding (Fab) and the receptor-binding (Fc) region. <sentence_start/>There are four subclasses of IgG, all of which share an overall structure homology but differ slightly in their amino acid sequence; the quantity of the subclasses in human serum is as follows: IgG1 > 2 > 3 > 4 (<citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="5443170" doi="10.1172/JCI106279" pmcid="PMC322522" count="1">2</citation>).

IgG3 represents ∼8% of the total amount of IgG in human serum (<citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="5443170" doi="10.1172/JCI106279" pmcid="PMC322522" count="1">2</citation>), and stands out from the other IgG subclasses for a number of reasons. <sentence_start/>First of all, IgG3 contains an elongated hinge region with up to a triple repeat sequence (the actual number ranging from one to three depending on the allotype (<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2014.00520" pmcid="PMC4202688" pmid="25368619" count="1">3</citation>)), which is responsible for the increased flexibility between the Fab and the Fc part, as well as the wider and more flexible angle between the two Fab arms (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9317136" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="3138110" doi="10.1002/j.1460-2075.1988.tb03037.x" pmcid="PMC454472" count="1">5</citation>). <sentence_start/>This flexibility is likely the cause of the increased affinity of IgG3, compared with the other subclasses, for divalent binding to certain types of antigens (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9317136" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11413323" doi="10.1128/JVI.75.14.6558-6565.2001" pmcid="PMC114379" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7561063" count="1">7</citation>). <sentence_start/>Second, IgG3 has a higher affinity for C1q, which initiates the classical complement pathway (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="3138110" doi="10.1002/j.1460-2075.1988.tb03037.x" pmcid="PMC454472" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9659234" doi="10.1046/j.1365-2567.1998.00472.x" pmcid="PMC1364140" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>The interaction between IgG3 and C1q is not due to the elongated hinge region, as demonstrated by studies showing that recombinant IgG3 with an IgG1- or IgG4-like hinge sequence exhibited even greater binding affinity for C1q than wild-type IgG3 (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9659234" doi="10.1046/j.1365-2567.1998.00472.x" pmcid="PMC1364140" count="1">8<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" pmid="1915551" doi="10.1002/eji.1830211013" count="1" /></citation>-<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18483271" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-07-6297" count="1">10</citation>). <sentence_start/>Third, IgG3 has a higher overall affinity for the Fcγ receptors (FcγRs), through which it can influence effector cells of the innate immune system (<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrd2909" pmid="22460124" count="1">11</citation>). <sentence_start/>The CH2 domain and hinge region of IgG3 were shown to be instrumental in binding to the high affinity FcγRI receptor (<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" pmid="1827828" doi="10.1084/jem.173.6.1483" pmcid="PMC2190830" count="1">12</citation>). <sentence_start/>Finally, IgG3 generally has a shorter half-life compared with the other IgG subclasses (1 <italic>versus</italic> 3 weeks) (<citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="5443170" doi="10.1172/JCI106279" pmcid="PMC322522" count="1">2</citation>). <sentence_start/>This difference was traced back to an H435R mutation that confers a positive charge at physiological pH, resulting in a decreased binding to the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), which is involved in recycling IgG targeted for lysosomal degradation (<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22186895" doi="10.1038/ncomms1608" pmcid="PMC3247843" count="1">13</citation>). <sentence_start/>The low-efficiency FcRn-mediated transport also gives rise to decreased levels of IgG3 in mucosal tissue and impaired transport of IgG3 across the placenta (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23829325" doi="10.1111/trf.12334" count="1">14</citation>). <sentence_start/>These properties do not hold true for all types of IgG3 since a large number of IgG3 allotypes have been described, some of which lack the H435R substitution and have a half-life and placental transport rates similar to IgG1 (<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22186895" doi="10.1038/ncomms1608" pmcid="PMC3247843" count="1">13<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23829325" doi="10.1111/trf.12334" count="1"><citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11781688" doi="10.1038/sj.ejhg.5200700" count="1" /></citation></citation>-<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20073133" doi="10.4161/mabs.1.4.9122" pmcid="PMC2726606" count="1">16</citation>). <sentence_start/>IgG3 is more polymorphic than the other IgG subclasses, as evidenced by the high number of known allotypes (<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20073133" doi="10.4161/mabs.1.4.9122" pmcid="PMC2726606" count="1">16</citation>). <sentence_start/>Most of the polymorphisms reside in the CH2 or CH3 domain, but the length of the hinge region can also display a high degree of variation. <sentence_start/>Depending on the number of sequence repeats, the hinge region can vary from 27 to 83 amino acid residues between different IgG3 allotypes (<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2014.00520" pmcid="PMC4202688" pmid="25368619" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20073133" doi="10.4161/mabs.1.4.9122" pmcid="PMC2726606" count="1">16</citation>, <citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9003512" doi="10.1007/s004390050328" count="1">17</citation>).

An <italic>N</italic>-linked complex type glycan is highly conserved and found in the CH2 domain of all IgG subclasses and allotypes. <sentence_start/>The type of glycan present at this site has been shown to influence the effector functions of IgG (<citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MOT.0b013e328342538f" pmid="21150612" count="1">18</citation>). <sentence_start/>N-glycans that lack a core fucose cause IgG to have an enhanced proinflammatory capacity through stronger binding to FcγRIIIa and FcγRIIIb (<citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MOT.0b013e328342538f" pmid="21150612" count="1">18<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M202069200" pmid="11986321" count="1" /></citation>-<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24243971" doi="10.1182/blood-2013-09-527978" pmcid="PMC3901064" count="1">20</citation>). <sentence_start/>In contrast, IgG carrying sialylated N-glycans exhibits anti-inflammatory properties, likely due to increased binding affinity to C-type lectins and/or reduced binding to FcγR (<citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MOT.0b013e328342538f" pmid="21150612" count="1">18</citation>, <citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16888140" doi="10.1126/science.1129594" count="1">21</citation>, <citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22922409" doi="10.1038/nm.2862" pmcid="PMC3492054" count="1">22</citation>).

O-linked glycosylation has been reported for various immunoglobulins. <sentence_start/>O-glycans are present on the hinge region of human IgA1 and IgD and mouse IgG2b (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7512967" count="1">23<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.273.4.2260" pmid="9442070" count="1" /></citation>-<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" pmid="6806818" doi="10.1073/pnas.79.9.2850" pmcid="PMC346304" count="1">25</citation>). <sentence_start/>IgA1 contains nine potential sites for O-glycosylation (serine and threonine) in the hinge region, of which 3-5 are occupied, while IgD has been reported to carry between four and seven O-glycans (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.273.4.2260" pmid="9442070" count="1">24<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" pmid="6806818" doi="10.1073/pnas.79.9.2850" pmcid="PMC346304" count="1" /></citation>-<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7092891" doi="10.1016/0006-291x(82)91078-6" count="1">26</citation>). <sentence_start/>The O-glycosylation in the hinge of murine IgG2b was observed to protect against proteolytic digestion (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7512967" count="1">23</citation>). <sentence_start/>Likewise, IgA1 was found to be more susceptible to degradation by <italic>Streptococci</italic> proteases after neuraminidase treatment (<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/iai.58.5.1186-1194.1990" pmcid="PMC258608" pmid="2182537" count="1">27</citation>).

In this study, we report partial O-glycosylation of the human IgG3 hinge. <sentence_start/>We obtained both poly- and monoclonal IgG3 from various sources and performed proteolytic digestion with trypsin or proteinase K. NanoLC-reverse phase (RP)-ESI-ion trap (IT)-MS/MS was used to examine the resulting (glyco)peptides, revealing core 1-type O-glycans on multiple sites within the IgG3 hinge region.
EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES
Immunoglobulin Sources
Polyclonal IgG3 from Donor Sera

IgG3 was purified from six serum samples (average donor age: 44.5 ± 9 years; three male and three female; details are listed in ). <sentence_start/>The serum samples were collected from healthy donors with informed consent in compliance with the institutional ethical board. <sentence_start/>Venous blood was collected in a 9-ml Vacuette serum clot activator tube (Greiner BioOne, Kremsmünster, Austria) and incubated at room temperature for 30 min, followed by centrifugation for 15 min at 1800 g. <sentence_start/>The serum fraction was then collected and stored at −20 °C. <sentence_start/>IgG was isolated by running the serum over a HiTrap Protein G HP column (GE Healthcare, Buckinghamshire, UK) and eluted with 0.1 <sc>m</sc> glycine-HCl, pH 2.7. <sentence_start/>The eluate containing IgG was then applied to a HiTrap MabSelect SuRE column packed with recombinant Protein A (GE Healthcare), and the IgG3-containing flow-through was concentrated using an Amicon Ultra-15 centrifugal filter device 10 kDa (Merck Millipore, Darmstadt, Germany) and dialyzed against PBS using a Slide-A-Lizer Dialysis Cassette, 10K MWCO (Dionex/Thermo Scientific, Sunnyvale, CA).
Polyclonal IgG3 from Pooled Plasma

IgG3 purified from pooled plasma was obtained commercially from Athens Research and Technology (Athens, GA). <sentence_start/>Upon inquiry, we learned that this IgG3 had been treated with dextran sulfate, followed by centrifugation to pellet the lipids. <sentence_start/>The delipidated plasma was then subjected to an ammonium sulfate precipitation, followed by boric acid precipitation. <sentence_start/>The IgG was isolated with ion exchange chromatography, and further purification of IgG3 was achieved with affinity chromatography (rProtein A), gel filtration chromatography, and a jacalin column to remove a minor IgA contaminant. <sentence_start/>This purification method did not expose the IgG3 to extreme pH conditions or temperatures above 55 °C.
Monoclonal IgG3

Two monoclonal recombinant anti-GDob1 IgG3 allotypes, G3m(g) and G3m(s), were produced in an HEK-293F FreeStyle cell line expression system (Life Technologies, Paisley, UK). <sentence_start/>IgG3m(s) was then purified with a HiTrap MabSelect SuRE column packed with recombinant Protein A (GE Healthcare), while IgG3m(g) was purified with a Protein G HiTrap HP column (GE Healthcare).
Monoclonal IgG3 Mutants

Three IgG3 G3m(g) hinge mutants were produced recombinantly, together with wild-type IgG3 G3m(g) as a control. <sentence_start/>The variable regions of the heavy and light chains (VH, VL) of the mouse IgG1 anti-2,4,6-trinitrophenol (TNP) hapten antibodies were cloned onto human IgG3 and kappa backbones, respectively, as described previously (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24243971" doi="10.1182/blood-2013-09-527978" pmcid="PMC3901064" count="1">20</citation>, <citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23637394" doi="10.1128/JVI.00493-13" pmcid="PMC3700286" count="1">28</citation>). <sentence_start/>Synthetic DNA encoding for IgG3 mutants, replacing the three threonines (T) and/or serines (S) with alanines (A), was generated as 5′-NheI and 3′Bsu36I fragments by GeneArt (Invitrogen). <sentence_start/>The NheI-Bsu36I fragments were ligated in anti-TNP IgG3 heavy chain replacing the corresponding fragment in the wild-type heavy chain. <sentence_start/>Antibodies were produced in the HEK-293F FreeStyle cell line expression system (Invitrogen) with cotransfection of vectors encoding p21, p27, and pSVLT genes as described (<citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23872061" doi="10.1016/j.ymeth.2013.07.018" count="1">29</citation>) to increase protein production. <sentence_start/>The antibodies were purified on a protein G HiTrap HP column (GE Healthcare) using the ÄKTAprime plus system (GE Healthcare) and dialyzed against PBS overnight.
Monoclonal IgG3/4 Fc Constructs

Four recombinant IgG3 and IgG4 Fc constructs were produced in a HEK-293F FreeStyle cell line (Invitrogen) and purified with a Protein G column (Protein G Sepharose 4 fast flow; GE Healthcare), as described by Rispens <italic>et al.</italic> (<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M113.541813" pmcid="PMC3937676" pmid="24425871" count="1">30</citation>). <sentence_start/>All constructs contained an IgG4 hinge region, together with either the CH2 and CH3 regions of two IgG3 allotypes (G3m(b)-Fc-h4 and G3m(c3c5)-Fc-h4) or the CH2 and CH3 regions of two IgG4 variants (IgG4-Fc-V397M and IgG4-Fc-V397M,K392N).
Polyclonal and Monoclonal IgG4

Several IgG4 samples were collected. <sentence_start/>A polyclonal IgG4 sample was affinity-purified from the plasma of a rheumatoid arthritis patient using anti-IgG4 coupled to Sepharose (clone MH164.4, Sanquin, Amsterdam, The Netherlands). <sentence_start/>A second IgG4 sample was enriched from the serum of a patient from the Leiden University Medical Center with an extremely high IgG4 serum titer (14.4 mg/ml). <sentence_start/>The serum was heat-inactivated and subjected to a 33% cut ammonium sulfate precipitation, followed by dialysis to decrease the salt content. <sentence_start/>The IgG4 was then enriched on a HiTrap DEAE Sepharose and a Superdex 200 column (GE Healthcare) using an ÄKTAprime plus chromatography system (GE Healthcare); IgG4-containing fractions were identified using ELISA and pooled. <sentence_start/>A monoclonal anti-TNP IgG4 sample produced in HEK cells was purified with a protein G column and dialyzed against PBS in the same way as described for the IgG3 mutants. <sentence_start/>In addition, we obtained a recombinant humanized IgG4 sample in the form of the therapeutic antibody natalizumab (Tysabri; Biogen Idec, Badehoevedorp, The Netherlands), which is produced in murine myeloma cells.
The protein sequences of the recombinant samples can be found in .
SDS-PAGE Analysis and Proteolytic Digestion

Five μg of the IgG samples was reduced with 2-beta-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) at 95 °C for 10 min. <sentence_start/>The IgG was then run on a NuPage 4-12% Bis-Tris SDS-PAGE gel (Invitrogen) and stained with Coomassie G-250 (SimplyBlue SafeStain, Invitrogen). <sentence_start/>Bands were excised, cut into pieces, washed with 25 m<sc>m</sc> ammonium bicarbonate (ABC<sup>1</sup>, Sigma-Aldrich), and dehydrated with acetonitrile (Biosolve, Valkenswaard, The Netherlands). <sentence_start/>The IgG was then again treated with a reducing agent by adding 50 μl of a 10 m<sc>m</sc> <sc>dl</sc>-dithiothreitol (DTT; Sigma-Aldrich) 25 m<sc>m</sc> ABC solution for 30 min at 55 °C. <sentence_start/>The gel pieces were subsequently dehydrated by the addition of acetonitrile. <sentence_start/>Alkylation of the cysteine residues was achieved by incubation with 50 μl of a 55 m<sc>m</sc> iodoacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich) 25 m<sc>m</sc> ABC solution in the dark for 20 min. <sentence_start/>The gel pieces were then washed with 25 m<sc>m</sc> ABC and dehydrated with acetonitrile. <sentence_start/>The washing and dehydration was repeated a second time, and the samples were subsequently dried down completely in a centrifugal vacuum concentrator (Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany).

For proteolytic digestion to take place, 30 μl of 25 m<sc>m</sc> ABC containing either trypsin (sequencing grade modified trypsin, Promega, Madison, WI), proteinase K (from <italic>Tritirachium album</italic>; Sigma-Aldrich) or chymotrypsin (sequencing grade from bovine pancreas, Roche Applied Sciences, Mannheim, Germany) was added to the dried gel pieces. <sentence_start/>An IgG:enzyme (w/w) ratio of 1:20 for trypsin, 1:3 for proteinase K and 1:20 for chymotrypsin was used. <sentence_start/>The samples were kept on ice for 1 h, to allow the enzyme to enter the gel pieces. <sentence_start/>If the gel pieces were not fully submerged, a further 10-20 μl of 25 m<sc>m</sc> ABC was added. <sentence_start/>The samples were incubated overnight at 37 °C. <sentence_start/>The solution surrounding the gel pieces was collected the next morning. <sentence_start/>Following the addition of another 20 μl of 25 m<sc>m</sc> ABC, the gel pieces were incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. <sentence_start/>The solution was then again collected and added to the first fraction, and stored at −20 °C.

Alternatively, several IgG3 samples were digested in solution without reduction alkylation: 3 μg of IgG3 was incubated with 0.3 μg of trypsin in a total volume of 25 μl 25 m<sc>m</sc> ABC at 37 °C overnight.

Endoproteinase AspN (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) was used to further digest trypsin-generated (glyco)peptides. <sentence_start/>Digestion was performed by adding 1.5 μl of AspN and 15 μl of 2x AspN buffer (100 m<sc>m</sc> Tris-HCl, 5 m<sc>m</sc> zinc sulfate, New England Biolabs) to 15 μl of trypsin-digested IgG3, and incubating overnight at 37 °C.
Exoglycosidase Digestion

Exoglycosidase digestion was performed on tryptic IgG glycopeptides. <sentence_start/>The trypsin-digested IgG3 was first heated to 95 °C for 5 min to inactivate the trypsin. <sentence_start/>The sample was then dried in a centrifugal vacuum concentrator (Eppendorf), and resuspended by the addition of 16 μl of Milli-Q-purified water, 2 μl 50 m<sc>m</sc> sodium acetate (pH 5.5), 1 μl sialidase (Glyko sialidase A, Prozyme, Hayward, CA), and 1 μl of galactosidase (Glyko beta-galactosidase, Prozyme). <sentence_start/>The samples were incubated overnight at 37 °C.
NanoLC-ESI-IT-MS(/MS) Analysis

The IgG3 (glyco)peptides were analyzed with nanoLC-reversed phase (RP)-electrospray (ESI)-ion trap (IT)-MS(/MS) on an Ultimate 3000 RSLCnano system (Dionex/Thermo Scientific) coupled to an amaZon speed ESI-IT-MS (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany). <sentence_start/>A precolumn (Acclaim PepMap C18 capillary column, 300 μm x 5 mm, particle size 5 μm, Dionex/Thermo Scientific) was used to wash and concentrate the sample, and separation was achieved on an Acclaim PepMap RSLC C18 nanocolumn (75 μm x 150 mm, particle size 2 μm, Dionex/Thermo Scientific) with a flow rate of 500 nl/min. <sentence_start/>The following linear gradient was used, with solvent A consisting of 0.1% formic acid in water and solvent B of 95% acetonitrile, 5% water: t = 0 min, 1% solvent B; t = 5 min, 1% B; t = 20 min, 25% B; t = 25 min, 70% B; t = 30 min, 70% B; t = 31 min, 1% B; t = 55 min, 1% B. <sentence_start/>The sample was ionized in positive ion mode with an ESI-nanosprayer (4500 V) using a bare fused silica capillary (internal diameter of 20 μm). <sentence_start/>The solvent was evaporated at 180 °C with a nitrogen flow of 5 liters/min. <sentence_start/>A CaptiveSpray nanoBooster (Bruker Daltonics) was mounted onto the mass spectrometer and saturated the nitrogen flow with ACN to enhance the sensitivity. <sentence_start/>The MS1 ion detection window was set at <italic>m/z</italic> 350-1400, and the MS2 window at <italic>m/z</italic> 140-2200. <sentence_start/>The three highest nonsingly charged peaks in each MS1 spectrum were automatically fragmented through collision-induced dissociation (CID). <sentence_start/>In order to identify the peptide sequence of proteinase K- and trypsin-generated O-glycopeptides, MS3 analysis was performed on manually selected precursors: the MS2 peak representing the peptide without sugars attached was targeted for fragmentation. <sentence_start/>In a separate LC-MS run, electron transfer dissociation fragmentation was done on selected precursor ions.
t-ITP-CE-ESI-qTOF-MS(/MS) Analysis

Transient isotachophoresis (ITP)-capillary electrophoresis (CE)-ESI-qTOF-MS/MS analysis was performed on a tryptic sialidase- and galactosidase-treated IgG3 sample derived from pooled plasma. <sentence_start/>Separation was achieved on a CESI 8000 system (AB Sciex, Framingham, MA), coupled via porous sheathless interfacing to an ultra-high resolution (UHR)-qTOF maXis Impact MS system (Bruker Daltonics) operating in positive ion mode. <sentence_start/>The sample migrated over a 90-cm bare fused capillary (i.d. 30 μm, o.d. 150 μm, AB Sciex). <sentence_start/>A 10% acetic acid solution was used as background electrolyte and a 50 m<sc>m</sc> ammonium acetate solution as leading electrolyte. <sentence_start/>A voltage of 20 kV was applied and 70 nl was injected during 1 min. <sentence_start/>The ion detection window for both MS1 and MS2 was set at <italic>m/z</italic> 50-2200.
Data Processing

The LC-MS(/MS) data was analyzed using DataAnalysis 4.2 software (Bruker Daltonics). <sentence_start/>Within this program, the function Compounds - AutoMS(n) was used to generate 300 compound spectra (with sum spectra generated for compounds within an <italic>m/z</italic> window of 0.5 Th over a chromatographic peak width of 0.5 min), and these data were deconvoluted and exported as a mascot generic file. <sentence_start/>Protein identification through primary sequence database searching was performed using the MASCOT search algorithm (MASCOT Daemon version 2.2.2; Matrix Science, London, UK). <sentence_start/>The following MASCOT settings were used: taxonomy: <italic>Homo sapiens</italic>; database: SwissProt; enzyme: trypsin (for trypsin digests)/no enzyme (for proteinase K digests)/chymotrypsin (for chymotrypsin digests); fixed modifications: carbamidomethyl (C); variable modifications: oxidation (M); max missed cleavages: 1; MS1 peptide tolerance: 0.3 Da; MS/MS tolerance: 0.3 Da; #13C: 0.

The fragmentation spectra were screened manually for common oxonium fragment ions, which are characteristic for glycopeptide fragmentation: <italic>m/z</italic> 366.14, [1 HexNAc (<italic>N</italic>-acetylhexosamine) + 1 Hex (hexose) + H]<sup>+</sup>; <italic>m/z</italic> 292.10, [1 NeuAc (<italic>N</italic>-acetylneuraminic acid) + H]<sup>+</sup>; <italic>m/z</italic> 274.09, [1 NeuAc - H<sub>2</sub>O + H]<sup>+</sup>; <italic>m/z</italic> 657.23, [1 HexNAc + 1 Hex + 1 NeuAc + H]<sup>+</sup>. <sentence_start/>From the MS/MS spectra of O-glycopeptides, the composition of the glycan and the mass of the peptide moiety could be deduced. <sentence_start/>This peptide mass was used to generate matching IgG peptide sequences using the ExPASY FindPept software tool ( ). <sentence_start/>The MS3 spectrum of the peptide moiety was then used to confirm the peptide sequence, by comparing the peaks in the spectrum to the b and y ions expected according to the Protein Prospector MS-Product tool ( ).

Relative quantification of the O-glycans present on the tryptic IgG3 peptide SCDTPPPCPR was done by summing LC-MS spectra over a fixed time window of 0.5 min surrounding the elution of each (glyco)peptide, and then summing the background-corrected intensities of the first 3 isotopic peaks for each O-glycopeptide. <sentence_start/>If the compound was present in multiple charge states, the background-corrected peak intensities of the different charge states were summed followed by normalizing the data so that the total was 100%. <sentence_start/>A separate correction factor was applied to each of the glycopeptides to correct for the fact that higher mass compounds have a lower percentage of signal intensity present in the first 3 isotopic peaks. <sentence_start/>First, the percentage of signal intensity present in each isotopic peak was calculated using IDCalc version 0.3 (University of Washington). <sentence_start/>The correction factor consists of the percentage of signal intensity present in the first three isotopic peaks of the peptide divided by the percentage of signal intensity present in the first three isotopic peaks of the O-glycopeptide.

In order to obtain a more accurate determination of the percentage of oligosaccharide occupation of the tryptic IgG3 peptide SCDTPPPCPR, relative quantification was done using LC-MS analysis of a sialidase- and galactosidase-treated tryptic digest sample. <sentence_start/>The ratio between the peptide and the peptide + HexNAc was determined in the same way as described above.

DISCUSSION

IgG3 stands out from the other IgG subclasses due to its elongated hinge region and enhanced effector functions. <sentence_start/>In this paper, we demonstrate for the first time partial O-glycosylation of threonine residues within the triple repeat sequence in the hinge region of each IgG3 heavy chain. <sentence_start/>Non-, mono- and disialylated core 1 type O-glycans were identified in IgG3 from various sources. <sentence_start/>A hexasaccharide disialylated O-glycan was also present at a very low abundance but only in the monoclonal IgG3 samples.
Relative Abundance and Distribution of IgG3 O-glycosylation

An estimate of the relative abundance of the various O-glycans was determined from nanoLC-ESI-IT-MS analysis of trypsin-generated (glyco)peptides. <sentence_start/>It should be noted that because the signal of the monosialylated O-glycopeptide in triply charged state overlapped with the doubly charged peak of the hinge repeat peptide with a putative acetylation modification in all samples, only the doubly charged signal of the monosialylated O-glycopeptide was quantified, thereby leading to an underestimation of this O-glycoform. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, it is known that glycopeptides with different glycan structures can have different response factors (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jms.3189" pmid="23776102" count="1">35</citation>), and thus the relative abundances we measured may not accurately reflect the real ratios. <sentence_start/>In order to obtain a more reliable estimate of the percentage of the hinge repeat motif bearing an O-glycan, tryptic IgG peptides were incubated with exoglycosidases, trimming all O-glycans down to a single <italic>N</italic>-acetylhexosamine. <sentence_start/>A previous study of quantitative measurements of a single glycosylated peptide using nanoLC-ESI-IT-MS found that the glycopeptide with a single <italic>N</italic>-acetylglucosamine produced signal strengths similar to the nonglycosylated peptide (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jms.3189" pmid="23776102" count="1">35</citation>). <sentence_start/>Given the structural similarities between <italic>N</italic>-acetylglucosamine and <italic>N</italic>-acetylgalactosamine, we expect our method of relative quantification of desialylated and degalactosylated O-glycopeptides to give a reliable estimate of the degree of O-glycosylation.

Approximately 10% of the hinge repeat threonines carry an O-glycan in polyclonal IgG3 derived from donor sera. <sentence_start/>Despite differences in the age and sex of the donors, the degree and type of O-glycosylation appears similar in all six samples. <sentence_start/>This is in contrast to the N-glycosylation profiles of these samples, which do show interindividual differences in agreement with the literature (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23298168" doi="10.1021/pr300887z" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the two monoclonal IgG3 allotypes, we examined, IgG3m(g) and IgG3m(s), ∼12-14% of the O-glycosylation sites were occupied; this increase may be due to the expression system (HEK cells) in which these antibodies were produced (<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jbiotec.2012.06.038" pmid="22814405" count="1">37</citation>).

A clear difference in O-glycosylation was seen between the commercially obtained IgG3 sample derived from pooled plasma and the other IgG3 samples: The former exhibited a much lower level of terminal <italic>N</italic>-acetylneuraminic acids per O-glycan, as well as a lower level of O-glycosylation overall. <sentence_start/>Two explanations could be found in the details of the preparation process that were supplied by the manufacturer of this IgG3 sample: Boric acid was used for precipitation and a jacalin column was used to remove a minor IgA contaminant. <sentence_start/>Acidic treatment has been known to cause loss of terminal N-acetylneuraminic acid (<citation rid="B38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9751791" doi="10.1093/glycob/8.11.1045" count="1">38</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the N-glycans of pooled-plasma-derived IgG3 did not show a decrease in sialylation compared with single-donor-derived IgG3, which makes it unlikely that boric acid treatment is responsible for the lower level of O-glycan sialylation. <sentence_start/>Jacalin is a plant lectin with affinity for core 1 type O-glycans; it binds O-glycosylated proteins such as IgA1, as well as several animal IgGs that are suspected of carrying O-glycosylation (<citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21964726" doi="10.1093/glycob/cwr099" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" pmid="1699452" doi="10.1016/0003-2697(90)90605-9" count="1">40</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, it has been reported that jacalin has a higher affinity for nonsialylated than for sialylated O-glycans in the case of fetuin (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" pmid="1699452" doi="10.1016/0003-2697(90)90605-9" count="1">40</citation>), and the same was observed for monoclonal IgG3 that was run over a jacalin column and found to be depleted for nonsialylated and partially depleted for monosialylated but not for disialylated O-glycans (unpublished data). <sentence_start/>This does not explain why the pooled plasma-derived IgG3 would exhibit lower levels of disialylated O-glycans and higher levels of monosialylated O-glycans compared with single donor serum-derived IgG3. <sentence_start/>In any case, it is difficult to say anything about possible depletion without being able to observe the O-glycosylation profile of the original non-jacalin-treated pooled plasma sample. <sentence_start/>Because it was shown that jacalin interacts with the O-glycosylated IgG3 hinge and because of the deviating O-glycosylation profile obtained from the jacalin-treated pooled plasma-derived sample <italic>versus</italic> IgG3 from single human donors obtained without jacalin depletion, the results obtained for this IgG3 sample will not be deemed representative for the overall human population.

It is likely that the O-glycosylation is distributed randomly among all IgG3s, since monoclonal cell cultures were found to produce partially O-glycosylated instead of either fully or non-O-glycosylated IgG3. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, hinge peptide-dimer repeats linked by interchain disulfide bridges rarely carry two O-glycans, which indicates that the O-glycosylation is not clustered on a subset of the IgG3 molecules. <sentence_start/>If the O-glycosylation is distributed randomly, approximately half (1 − probability of 6 unoccupied sites = 1 − ((1 − 0.10)^6) = 47%) of the IgG3s would be expected to carry at least one O-glycan. <sentence_start/>We observed that less than 1% of hinge peptide-dimer repeats carried two disialylated O-glycans in monoclonal IgG3 samples, whereas the expected value assuming random O-glycosylation site occupancy would be ∼3.8% (G3m(g)) and 2.8% (G3m(s)). <sentence_start/>These findings indicate that addition of O-linked glycans is inhibited if a glycan is already present at the adjacent site on the opposing heavy chain, thus dispersing the O-glycosylation across a higher percentage of IgG3s.
Criteria Determining IgG Hinge-Region O-glycosylation

Based on the amino acid sequence of the IgG3 hinge repeat region, it is not surprising that it forms a target for O-glycosylation. <sentence_start/>It is known that O-glycosylation occurs in sequences with a high abundance of proline residues, preferentially at position −1 and +3 relative to the glycosylation site (<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" pmid="2025231" doi="10.1042/bj2750529" pmcid="PMC1150083" count="1">41</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the IgG3 hinge repeat, six of the 16 amino acid residues consist of prolines, including one at position +3 relative to the glycosylation site. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, due to its extended formation, the IgG3 hinge region has a high degree of surface accessibility (<citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3083.1975.tb02607.x" pmid="1145126" count="1">42</citation>), which is also associated with O-glycosylation (<citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15385431" doi="10.1093/glycob/cwh151" count="1">43</citation>). <sentence_start/>Surface accessibility may be responsible for the slightly lower degree of O-glycosylation observed in recombinant IgG3m(s) compared with m(g): the shorter length of the hinge region of IgG3m(s), which contains two hinge repeats instead of three, could decrease the accessibility for glycosyltransferases. <sentence_start/>No O-glycosylation was observed at the threonine residues at the N-terminal end of the hinge, T<sub>H1-4</sub>,T<sub>H1-9</sub> and T<sub>H1-10</sub>, which may be due to either the local amino acid sequence or the secondary structure of this region.

O-glycosylation was also found to be present on the IgG4 hinge of Fc constructs with IgG4 or IgG3 CH2 and CH3 domains. <sentence_start/>This is not surprising considering the high abundance of proline residues (at position −4, −3, −1, 2, and 4 relative to O-glycosylation site S228) in the IgG4 hinge region, which are a well-known marker for O-glycosylation (<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" pmid="2025231" doi="10.1042/bj2750529" pmcid="PMC1150083" count="1">41</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, intact IgG4, whether purified from serum or expressed in the same HEK cell expression system as the Fc constructs, was not found to carry hinge region O-glycosylation. <sentence_start/>It is therefore likely that the presence of the Fab fragment influences the accessibility of the hinge region, preventing the attachment of an O-glycan in the Golgi apparatus in the case of intact IgG4. <sentence_start/>Similarly, O-glycosylation was recently reported on an IgG1 Fc-fragment produced in HEK and CHO cells but not on intact IgG1 produced under the same circumstances (<citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jmb.2014.07.006" pmcid="PMC4159253" pmid="25036289" count="1">44</citation>). <sentence_start/>This reinforces the notion that accessibility is essential for the attachment of O-glycans (<citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15385431" doi="10.1093/glycob/cwh151" count="1">43</citation>). <sentence_start/>For human IgG3, this is provided by the extensive length of its IgG3 hinge, which in the intact IgG molecules for other IgG subclasses is shielded by the Fab fragments.
Function of IgG3 O-glycosylation

The function of the O-glycans found on the IgG3 hinge region has not been investigated, but previous findings give rise to several options. <sentence_start/>First, the hinge glycosylation might prohibit proteolytic degradation. <sentence_start/>The IgG hinge is the target of a number of bacterial or endogenous proteases (<citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20400859" doi="10.4161/mabs.2.3.11780" pmcid="PMC2881249" count="1">45</citation>, <citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19815504" doi="10.1073/pnas.0904174106" pmcid="PMC2758810" count="1">46</citation>), and the extended structure of the IgG3 hinge is presumably the reason that IgG3 is more susceptible to proteolytic degradation than the other IgG subclasses (<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-3083.1980.tb00039.x" pmid="6902981" count="1">47<citation rid="B48" ref-type="bibr" pmid="4113947" doi="10.1016/0019-2791(71)90478-2" count="1" /></citation>-<citation rid="B49" ref-type="bibr" pmcid="PMC1712889" pmid="4924105" count="1">49</citation>). <sentence_start/>We found that tryptic IgG3 O-glycopeptides were resistant against endoprotease AspN digestion, while the corresponding nonglycosylated peptides were not, thus providing evidence that the hinge region O-glycans can shield the hinge region from proteolytic cleavage. <sentence_start/>In contrast, we did not observe any evidence of incomplete trypsin digestion in the form of miscleaved O-glycopeptides. <sentence_start/>O-glycosylation has also been found to mediate protease resistance in other immunoglobulins, such as mouse IgG2b and IgA (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7512967" count="1">23</citation>, <citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/iai.58.5.1186-1194.1990" pmcid="PMC258608" pmid="2182537" count="1">27</citation>). <sentence_start/>Another function for the hinge region oligosaccharides could consist of helping the hinge region maintain an extended conformation, which might contribute to the flexibility and orientation of the Fab fragments and thereby influence divalent binding to target antigens.

Furthermore, it could be speculated that deviations in the O-glycosylation of IgG3 may have pathological effects, as has been described for IgA nephropathy (<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10393701" doi="10.1172/JCI5535" pmcid="PMC408399" count="1">50</citation>). <sentence_start/>Aberrant glycosylation of IgA1 is known to play a causal role in IgA nephropathy: The truncated O-glycans are recognized by immunoglobulins, leading to the formation of antibody complexes that are deposited on blood vessel walls near the glomerulus (<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10393701" doi="10.1172/JCI5535" pmcid="PMC408399" count="1">50</citation>, <citation rid="B51" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25071157" doi="10.1074/mcp.M114.039693" pmcid="PMC4223494" count="1">51</citation>). <sentence_start/>A similar mechanism involving IgG3 O-glycosylation could be theorized to play a role in IgG nephropathy. <sentence_start/>It has been shown that patients with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, a subtype of primary glomerulopathy, have IgG deposits that consist predominantly of IgG3, which may be in line with a causal role for IgG3 O-glycosylation (<citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8995742" doi="10.1038/ki.1997.32" count="1">52</citation>). <sentence_start/>Further research is required to determine the exact nature and functional consequences of IgG3 hinge glycosylation.
